milestones.name: The owner picks the game's name, premise and look from three or more concepts, each shown with its own art in a crowded arena
milestones.quality_bar: Minimum requirements only, because these options exist for the owner to turn some down: each concept is complete, original, made the way the finished game's art would be made, and different in kind from the others. The full bar starts with the chosen concept, from M2 on.

items.statement: At least three concepts each have a name, a paragraph of premise, one hero sprite, two enemy sprites, a palette, and a mock arena of 1920×1080 pixels in which 2,000 enemies surround the hero, a common enemy's body being no more than a fiftieth of the image's height. Every sprite's source, a script or an image file, is in `examples/swarm/concepts/`. One image, `docs/evidence/SWARM/concepts.png`, lays the concepts side by side with each sprite at game size and enlarged.
items.ask: Read the check and the script that composes the mocks. Is the count of enemies taken from the placements the composer drew, and the body size from the sprites it used? Is each mock composed with premultiplied alpha in linear light, as the design says the engine draws?

items.statement: The concepts differ in kind: each has its own premise and its own way of drawing, and no two are one idea in other colours. In each mock arena the hero can be found among the 2,000 and the two enemies can be told apart at the size shown.
items.inspect: Open `docs/evidence/SWARM/concepts.png` and each mock arena at 1920×1080. Judge each mock whole, at the size it is shown, and in native-size crops around the hero and of a patch of crowd. Judge only whether the concepts differ in kind and whether each reads at game size; which is best is the owner's.

items.statement: Every concept is original. No name, character, sprite or palette is taken from an existing game or from Broadsides, and no file comes from a third party unless it is public domain or CC0 and listed with its source.
items.ask: Does `examples/swarm/concepts/SOURCES.md` list, for each concept's name, the search that was made for a shipped game or studio of that name and what it found, and for each image file how it was made? Does any concept's hero, enemy or premise reproduce a character of Vampire Survivors, Brotato, Halls of Torment, Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor or another game you can name?

items.statement: The owner has picked one concept. The pick, and anything the owner asked to change, is written in `examples/swarm/CONCEPT.md` as the reference later milestones are judged against: the name, the premise, and the qualities of the look in words.
items.inspect: Read the recorded Human Feedback beside `examples/swarm/CONCEPT.md`. Does the file say what the owner chose and every change they asked for, and nothing they did not say?

needs.what: Look at the concepts laid side by side and pick one, or say what to change. Enemies are drawn this small because thousands must fit on screen; say so if you would rather have fewer and larger.

milestones.name: One hero holds out alone against a crowd that grows into the thousands, with attacks that fire on their own, on the Mac and in Chrome
milestones.quality_bar: A crowd as dense and as legible as Vampire Survivors' or Halls of Torment's late game, at several times their count: the hero is found at a glance, every hit shows, and nothing stutters. The look is the concept the owner picked, in `examples/swarm/CONCEPT.md`.

items.statement: Chrome's cost at each crowd size is on record before the cap is chosen. In Chrome at 1920×1080, with this milestone's rules and drawing and a crowd packed as the slice's late crowd packs, the record holds the median tick, the median frame's CPU work and their sum at each thousand bodies from 2,000 to 10,000, the cap the rule set uses, and each tripwire the design names that a row trips. The figures are baselines: none sets the cap and none decides the result.
items.ask: Were the figures taken in the game itself (its rules, row extraction, ordering and draw submission) as release Wasm on the page's one thread in Chrome, at the claimed commit, with the load on the machine recorded? Does the command succeed or fail on the record being complete and made at the claimed commit, and never on a figure?

items.statement: The slice's rules hold. A hero moves by the frame's axes, clamped to unit length, and stays inside the arena. Enemies seek the nearest hero and push apart, and never move a hero. A weapon fires on its own clock at the nearest enemies, a projectile hits the first enemy its path overlaps, health and damage are integers, a dead enemy despawns, and a hero whose health is spent ends the run. The spawn budget rises with time and the world never holds more bodies than the cap, a constant of the rule set of at most 10,000.
items.ask: Read the test. Does it step the registered runtime with the real rules, and check each clause from committed state: a hero's position unchanged by any number of enemies in contact, a weapon's hit against a brute-force search over the bodies, and the body count against the cap on every tick of a run that reaches it?

items.statement: On the Mac, the slice's retained trace, a run alone that reaches the cap, steps to its retained digests by the local route and by the wire route.
items.ask: Does the command run `SIM-2D`'s conformance command on the `swarm-rules` package, with no copy of its comparison? Do the trace's frames hold axes off the wire's 16-bit grid?

items.statement: In Chrome, as Wasm, the same trace steps to the same retained digests.
On the iPhone simulator the same trace steps to the same retained digests.
A slice of the trace runs inside the project's test command on the Mac, so a change to any rule's result fails at once.

`swarm-rules` is registered as a rule package and passes `SIM-2D`'s guard with nothing suppressed. The repository guard admits the game as a second external game: no engine crate may depend on either game, and the V1 game's boundary is as it was.
items.ask: Does `.config/architecture.toml` name the game's packages as a second external game, with `swarm-rules` as a rule package? Do the repository guard's own tests refuse an engine crate that depends on either game and a rule package that depends on a package which is not one? Did any line of the V1 game's boundary change?

items.statement: In a 16:9 view, during the last quarter of the trace, at least 2,000 enemies and projectiles are inside the player's view at one tick, counted from committed positions against the rectangle the view gives a 16:9 window.

On the Mac the game runs the trace in its own window through the 2D scene, in a landscape, a portrait and a square window. In each, the world's digests at the trace's checkpoints equal the run with no window, every living body has a row in the frame's record, no enemy the budget spawned has a first row that touches the view of its frame, and the compiled passes are the sprite pass and the output half's and nothing else. The run carries on by digest through a resize from landscape to portrait during a wave and through a replaced device.

In Chrome the game runs the trace on its page through the 2D scene, in a landscape and a portrait page, with the same digests at the checkpoints, a row for every living body, and no enemy the budget spawned having a first row that touches the view of its frame. The run carries on by digest through a resize between the two shapes during a wave and through a replaced device.

On the Mac, at the trace's peak, these are on record at 1920×1080 and at 3456×2234 from release builds with the load on the machine: the tick and its parts, with neighbours visited; rows extracted, ordered and uploaded; frame CPU and GPU time; and bodies in view. The record flags each tripwire the design names that a row trips. The figures are baselines: none decides the result.
items.ask: Does the command succeed or fail on the record being complete and made at the claimed commit, and never on a figure?

items.statement: In Chrome, at the trace's peak, the same rows are on record at 1920×1080.

On the Mac, at the peak of the slice, the player finds the hero at a glance, enemies stand apart from the ground and from each other, each shot and each hit shows, the overlap order of the crowd holds still, and the motion has no visible stutter or hitch.
items.inspect: Capture the trace's last quarter at 1920×1080 with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode, and `fixed` stills of three of its ticks at 3456×2234. Judge consecutive frames at 1x, whole and in native-size crops around the hero and of a packed patch of crowd, against the concept the owner picked, in `examples/swarm/CONCEPT.md`.

items.statement: In Chrome, at the peak of the slice, the same qualities hold.
items.inspect: Capture the trace's last quarter at 1920×1080 in Chrome with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode. Judge consecutive frames at 1x, whole and in native-size crops around the hero and of a packed patch of crowd.

items.statement: No engine crate names anything of the game, the game reaches the engine through public items alone, and nothing the game draws is written to the world.
items.ask: Does any crate under `crates/` name a type, constant, string or file of the game? Does `swarm` or `swarm-rules` use a non-public item of an engine crate? Does any code outside `swarm-rules` write a component or resource the digest covers? What did this milestone change in `thrum-app` and the capture and packaging scripts under seam ruling 2, and does each change serve any game?

Enemies appear only out of sight, by the rules' own figures. On every tick of a run that reaches the cap, with the hero in the open, at a wall and in a corner, every enemy the budget spawns is placed inside the arena and outside the hero's sight square grown by the spawn margin. The spawn rule is given committed state, admitted frames and the rule set's constants, and nothing of any window.
items.ask: Read the test and the spawn rule. Is each enemy's place read from committed state at its first tick and compared with the hero's committed place that the rule read? Is there any path by which a window's extent, a scale or a view could reach `swarm-rules`?

items.statement: Every view lies inside its hero's sight square. For window shapes from 32:9 to 9:32, the view the game gives shows exactly the sight spans at 16:9 and at 9:16, less along one side and no more along the other at every other shape, and stays inside the committed hero's sight square however far ahead the drawn hero is and wherever in the arena it stands, at a wall included.
items.ask: Is the view the game hands the renderer, in the Mac window and on the page, made by the one function this test calls, with the sight spans and the view slack read from `swarm-rules`?

milestones.name: A player plays a whole run alone on the Mac or in Chrome: waves that grow, upgrades chosen between them, a win or a loss, with the status display and menus
milestones.quality_bar: A run with the shape and clarity of Brotato's: a player always knows which wave they are in, how long it has left and what they just chose. Screens as plain and quick as Vampire Survivors' and Brotato's, in the look of the concept the owner picked, in `examples/swarm/CONCEPT.md`.

items.statement: The run is a state machine in the world: gathering, wave, intermission, won and lost. A state changes only at a tick or for an admitted action. Each wave's budget is larger than the last, and the last wave has a boss. An action that makes no sense in the state it meets changes nothing. A new run after a win or a loss differs from the last and is the same on any replay of the same inputs.
items.ask: Read the test. Is every transition driven through admitted frames and ticks alone, and is each kind of senseless action (a choice not offered, a hero picked twice, ready during a wave) tried in every state with the digest required unchanged?

items.statement: Pick-ups from anyone raise one team level, and each level gives each hero one owed choice. At an intermission each owed choice is an offer of three upgrades held in the world, the same on any replay. A choice is applied once. For every upgrade in the game, a run in which it was chosen differs at a later tick from the same run without it, in something other than the upgrade's own record.
items.ask: Does the test walk every upgrade the content tables declare, and compare state that play depends on (a body's position, health, a hit, a count), not the hero's list of upgrades?

items.statement: A pick-up within a hero's reach flies to it and is collected. Pick-ups left when a wave ends go to the pool. When many lie close they merge into one of their summed worth, the pool's total is unchanged by merging, and the world stays within the cap with pick-ups counted.
Over twenty seeds, a hero who never moves or chooses loses every run, and the scripted player wins at least one. How far each got in every seed, and how each run ended, is on record.
items.ask: Is the scripted player a fixed policy that reads only the committed page, with no knowledge of a seed? Are the twenty seeds listed in the record and not chosen after the runs?

items.statement: On the Mac a retained trace of a whole winning run, at most 36,000 ticks long, steps to its retained digests by the local and the wire route.
In Chrome the same trace steps to the same retained digests.

On the Mac, with events entering where the window's own do, a player goes from the title through a hero pick, a wave, an intermission in which one upgrade is chosen by keys and one by pointer, the pause menu, a win, a second run and a loss. Each activation reaches the rules as exactly one action, nothing the interface consumed moves the hero, a direction held through the end of a wave neither chooses a card nor is lost, and the pause menu holds the world and resumes it. The status display's health, wave, clock, level and count equal the committed world's at each checked frame.
items.ask: Are the status display's values read back from the interface tree and compared with the committed page of the same frame? Are the actions counted from what the rules were handed?

items.statement: In Chrome, with key, mouse and touch events sent through the browser, the same journey passes, with one upgrade chosen by each of the three means.

On the Mac a run carries on by digest, with the same screen open and focus where it was, through a resize, a device replaced during a wave and during an intermission, and a lost window focus, which releases held movement.
In Chrome a run carries on by digest, with the same screen open and focus where it was, through a resize, a replaced device and a tab hidden and shown.
One command starts the game on the Mac and one serves it to Chrome, each cooking the game's sheets and font first.

No element covers another, no text is cut off, and the status display stays legible over light and dark ground and a packed crowd.

items.statement: In real time on the Mac the end of a wave, the offer opening, a choice, and the next wave starting read as clean and immediate: nothing flickers or is drawn half laid out, the cleared field and the new wave are unmistakable, and the hero does not twitch.
items.inspect: Capture a scripted wave end, intermission and wave start at 1920×1080 with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode, with the event times from the run's record. Judge the consecutive frames around each event at 1x, whole and in native-size crops of the cards and the hero.

A run ends at one tick, won or lost. It is won at the tick the boss dies, or at the tick the last wave's clock ends with a present hero standing, and no intermission follows the last wave. It is lost at the tick a slot is present and no present hero stands. On a shared tick the boss's death beats the loss, and the loss beats the clock. Waiting spends no wave's clock: a player alone who waits in an intermission for more than 36,000 ticks and then readies meets the next wave with its whole clock.
items.ask: Read the test. Does it reach the last wave's deadline with the boss alive, once with a hero standing and once with the last hero falling on that very tick, and a boss death on the tick the last hero falls, and read each outcome from committed state? Does the wait step the real rules for every one of its ticks?

milestones.name: Four scripted players share one run on a simulated bad connection: every copy of the game stays identical, a player joins mid-run, one drops and returns, and upgrades are chosen together
milestones.quality_bar: Co-op rules as forgiving as Vampire Survivors' and Brotato's: nobody waits on anybody, nobody is left behind, and a friend can arrive or vanish at any moment without the run noticing.

items.statement: On the in-memory link, in virtual time, a host and four clients each step the game's rules in a world of their own through a wave and an intermission, and each client's digest equals the host's at every digest tick. It runs inside the project's test command.
items.ask: Does each peer hold its own registered runtime, reached by the others only through `thrum-network`'s session over the link? Does each peer record its own digests?

items.statement: On the in-memory link under A0's profile and under the harsh one, a host and four scripted players play a whole run at the cap. Each client's digest equals the host's at every digest tick, every peer reaches the run's end at the same tick, and after the first 600 ticks at least 95% of ticks admit each player's own frame.
items.ask: Is this `SESSION`'s match harness and its scripted-player seam running the game's rules, with no copy of the session or the link in the game?

items.statement: A player who joins after the first intermission picks a hero, which enters at one tick on every peer and holds one owed choice for each team level. A player whose link is cut has their hero leave the field at one tick on every peer, and returning with their token finds the same hero with everything it had. A slot that has left is free and its hero is gone. The spawn budget follows the number of present heroes from the tick of each event. Through all of it every peer's digest equals the host's at every digest tick.

The co-op rules hold. A fallen hero stays where it fell, neither moving nor firing, until the wave ends, and stands at the next wave with half its health. The run is lost at the tick a slot is present and no present hero stands. An intermission ends at the tick every present slot is ready, or when its clock runs out while more than one slot is present, and each owed choice then left is made by the rules. With every slot away the wave's clock and the budget hold, and with every slot left the world returns to gathering. With four heroes spread across the arena, every enemy the budget spawns is placed outside the sight square, grown by the spawn margin, of every present hero, standing or down.

Choices issued into loss and into a stalled link happen once, in order, on every peer. A choice made while another player's join is under way is applied at one tick on every peer, the joiner included. A choice that arrives after its intermission has closed changes nothing on any peer.

The hero's movement is one function that the movement rule and the predicted controller both call, and it is given nothing of the crowd. Over a whole run at the cap in which the hero is in contact with enemies throughout and falls at least once, the prediction equals the confirmed hero tick for tick wherever the host admitted the player's frame. Every correction is for one of four causes on record: a tick the host held, a change of lead, an upgrade to the hero's speed, or a change in whether the hero is standing (a fall, standing again, leaving or entering the field). Each change in standing corrects once.
items.ask: Does the test's hero spend the run in the crowd and fall in it? Does the test count corrections by cause from the session's own report, telling a change in standing from the controller's state before and after?

items.statement: The game declares its rule set, its action wire and which actions are commands to the session, and movement is the only thing it sends as timed frames.
items.ask: Which of the game's actions travel as commands and which as timed frames? Could losing any one timed frame lose a choice? Does the game's rule-set identity change when a constant of `swarm-rules` changes, with no other edit?

items.statement: From a whole run at the cap on the in-memory link under A0's profile these are on record: bytes each way for each peer, the lead and the confirmed delay, corrections a minute, the game's world image size at the cap and at a quarter of it, and the time from hello to in step for a join at the peak, split into transfer and catch-up. The record flags each tripwire the design names that a row trips. The figures are baselines: none decides the result.

milestones.name: A player hosting on this Mac and a friend who opens a link in Chrome play a run together over a real connection, each hero answering at once
milestones.quality_bar: Joining as plain as Factorio's or Stardew Valley's: a link, a short wait that says what it is doing, and you are in. Play that feels local for your own hero, as Factorio's latency hiding does, with the same crowd on both screens.

items.statement: A world can be driven. With a scripted driver in virtual time, the game's host and client worlds commit exactly the ticks the driver names at each advance (none, one, or several up to the cap on catch-up), draw at the interpolation the driver gives, and raise no overload for ticks nobody asked for. A world on the fixed clock behaves as before.
items.ask: Where was the driven world built under seam ruling 4? Does anything added to `thrum-core`, `thrum-render` or `thrum-app` for it name a session, a link or the game? Do the fixed-clock world's existing tests pass unchanged?

items.statement: Over real sockets, a Mac process that hosts and plays in its window and a Chrome page that joined by opening the host's link play a scripted whole run, directly and through the relay under A0's profile. Each peer's digest equals the other's at every digest tick and both reach the run's end at the same tick. The two windows differ in shape, one landscape and one portrait, and no enemy the budget spawned first appears inside either peer's view, by each peer's own record of its view.
items.ask: Are the two peers separate processes on `thrum-transport`'s sockets, with the relay's forwarded and dropped counts in the record? Is Chrome started with no flag that touches certificates, QUIC or origins? Does each peer write its own digests?

items.statement: A second Mac process joins a Mac host by a ticket given as a launch argument, and by a paste where the system lets the shell read the clipboard, and plays the run with equal digests. milestones.name: Two to four players on a Mac, in Chrome and on the iPhone simulator play a whole run together through delay and loss, the owner has played and accepted it, and track 3 is closed
milestones.quality_bar: The finished game: it would pass beside Vampire Survivors, Brotato, Halls of Torment and Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor in how it reads and moves, and beside Vampire Survivors' online co-op in how four players share a run. The look is the concept the owner picked, in `examples/swarm/CONCEPT.md`.

items.statement: Over real sockets through the relay under A0's profile, a headless host on the Mac and four players of the game (a Mac window, a second Mac process, a Chrome page and the app in the iPhone simulator) play a whole run. Every peer's digest equals the host's at every digest tick it reached, and every peer still in step sees the run end at the same tick. A peer the host closed as unable to keep up is on record with the reason and counts as no failure for the simulator. No enemy the budget spawned first appears inside any windowed peer's view, by each peer's own record of its view.
items.ask: Is each of the four the game itself built for its target, in its own process, with its platform and runtime version in the record? Did the Mac window and the Chrome page stay in step for the whole run?

items.statement: Two more mixes play a run with equal digests: two players, a Chrome page and the simulator app, on a headless host; and three, a Mac player who hosts in a window with a Chrome page and the simulator app joined. The simulator app joins from an address it is opened with.

With the windowed players under A0's profile: one joins in the third wave and enters beside the others; one loses its link for longer than the idle timeout and returns to its hero; one falls and stands at the next wave; and an intermission ends on its clock with one player's choices made for them. Every peer's digest equals the host's throughout.

With four heroes on screen each player tells their own from the others at a glance, and a fallen hero, an away hero, a hero entering and the other players' progress through an offer each read without explanation.

items.statement: Played alone on the Mac from the title to a win, the game holds its bar the whole way: each wave reads as larger than the last, the late crowd is thousands and stays legible, every weapon and upgrade a player takes shows in play, and nothing stutters, flickers or is left unfinished.
